Chapter 3: Facing Failure and Visualizing Risk
You know, there’s a certain comfort in imagining yourself succeeding. Most of us are encouraged to set goals and picture ourselves reaching them—seeing that big win in our minds. But in the world of spaceflight, there’s another side to this coin. It’s just as important, maybe even more so, to imagine what could go wrong.
Now, this isn’t about being negative or expecting the worst. It’s about being honest about the risks, and preparing for them so you can actually make success possible.
Think about what it takes to get ready for a spacewalk. The stakes are sky-high—literally. The environment out there? Totally unforgiving. So before anyone even thinks about leaving the safety of a spacecraft, astronauts put in endless hours rehearsing every possible scenario you can imagine.
They picture the suit springing a leak. They run through what happens if the tools slip out of their hands, or if the tether that keeps them attached comes loose. Each one of these possible failures gets picked apart, talked through, and planned for. The idea isn’t to get stuck worrying about disaster—it’s to make sure that, if something does go sideways, there’s already a plan in place.
And this way of thinking goes even further than just the technical stuff. There’s a great example—a crew member, after months of intense prep, suddenly gets the news: the mission’s been delayed. That disappointment? It’s real, and it stings. But instead of letting frustration take over, the focus shifts. What can be learned from this setback?
Time that could’ve been lost to disappointment gets put to good use—refining skills, building stronger relationships with the team, and getting ready for the next shot.
Most of us, honestly, try to avoid thinking about failure. It’s uncomfortable. Maybe even a little scary. But when you face it head-on, something changes. Suddenly, failure loses some of its power over you. When you’ve already imagined the worst-case scenario, made a plan for it, and even rehearsed it, it’s no longer paralyzing. It just turns into another challenge you can handle.
And this mindset? It’s not just for astronauts. Anyone who’s ever thought about making a big change—like switching careers, moving to a new city, or just taking a leap into the unknown—knows that fear of failure. But if you take the time to really imagine what could go wrong, and come up with real plans to deal with it, you’ll find you can move forward with a lot more confidence.
There’s also a powerful lesson here about resilience. Failure’s going to happen, no matter how prepared you are. The key is to treat every setback as a chance to learn something new. After every mission, astronauts sit down and go over everything. What worked? What could’ve been better? It’s not about pointing fingers—it’s about getting just a little bit better every time.
So, what’s the real value in visualizing failure? It’s not just about avoiding disaster. It’s about building rock-solid confidence—the kind that comes from knowing that, no matter what happens, you’ll find a way through. When you turn fear into action and setbacks into stepping stones, you’re not just preparing for the worst. You’re opening the door to your best possible outcome.
